name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
strategy: Long the two physical bottlenecks of the AI buildout at the cheap end of the multiple axis - memory/storage bits and merchant electrons - with the high-multiple, back-half-loaded silicon and optics legs removed and no leverage or short book.
reassessment_note: Two things changed this week and both point the same way. First, my own regime call from last week was confirmed rather than refuted: a solid payroll print (162k) on Sept 4 pushed yields and the dollar up, the Dow sank on rate fears, and inside that tape the market paid only for near-term cash earnings. MU (7.07x forward) rose 9.0% on the week to $1,016.59; AMAT fell 13.7% over the month, AVGO fell 14.9%, COHR 15.7%, FN 25.1%, and CRDO fell 26.7% in five sessions after BEATING on Q1 FY27 ($479M rev, $1.20 EPS) and guiding Q2 to $525-535M. Broadcom did the identical thing on Sept 2 - revenue $29.6B, up 86% year over year, guided $34.8B against $35.0B consensus, stock -6%. When a company grows 86% and the stock falls on a 0.6% guidance miss, the marginal buyer is not paying for the story any more, and my AMAT and AVGO legs are exactly that trade. They go. Second, the money that left is visibly arriving somewhere specific: Bridgewater more than doubled Vistra while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel disclosed $59M in VST, VST's CEO bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% decline, Microsoft and Meta signed multi-decade nuclear supply deals, and CEG signed ~1GW of long-term nuclear contracts and raised FY26 EPS guidance to $11.50-12.50. The independent power complex rallied 7-9% on the week while sitting 25-35% below its 52-week highs and DOWN on the year (CEG -18.0%, VST -9.4%, TLN -20.1%). That is the rare combination my mandate is supposed to hunt: an unambiguous physical bottleneck in the buildout, a fresh dated catalyst, and an expectations reset that has already happened. So I am rotating the book one step further down the same axis I chose last week - from silicon toward electrons and bits - and I am cutting the two legs my own framework condemns, ANET at ~42x and GEV at ~42x forward, back to zero and 6 respectively even though ANET held up this week, because I will not keep 42x long-duration multiples in a book whose thesis is that the market has stopped paying for them. I am also closing the CoreWeave short. It is down 5.27% on the leg and the reason it existed is gone: CRWV printed $2.58B of Q2 revenue up 112%, Truist raised to $165, it rose 5.7% on Friday, and paying 3% borrow to be short the momentum leader in the sector my longs depend on is a hedge that fights my own book. I would rather hold 26% in cash at 4% than run a short I no longer believe. Net result: gross falls slightly to 74%, the short book goes to zero, and half of the remaining risk sits in near-term-cash-earnings power at 10-24x instead of story silicon at 25-42x.

positions.thesis: The cheapest asset in the entire AI complex and the one the tape actually rewarded this week: $1,016.59 after +9.0% on the week, 7.07x forward earnings, 48 analysts at Strong Buy with a $1,513 average target (+48.8%). Memory is now named by NVIDIA itself as the strategic constraint on the buildout, and Micron is the only US-listed pure claim on DRAM/HBM bit scarcity. I am trimming from 22% to 20% rather than adding despite the momentum, because this is +222% year to date, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has been selling, David Tepper cut 41%, and China's CXMT just IPO'd with a 466% pop - the supply response is now visible on the horizon even if it is years from bits. So: still the largest leg, but with a 35% take-profit to force me to harvest a blow-off rather than round-trip one, and an 18% stop that is tighter than the 20% it carried before.

The best risk-reward on the board and the single clearest expression of this week's rotation. 14.50x forward earnings against a $217.42 consensus target (+45.6%, Strong Buy, 20 analysts), Q2 adjusted EBITDA up more than 30% year over year with 2026-2027 guidance reaffirmed, and the stock still 31% below its 52-week high and -9.4% year to date. The confirming evidence is who is buying: Bridgewater more than doubled its position while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel's fund disclosed $59M, and CEO James Burke bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% drawdown. This is a near-term-cash-earnings asset selling electrons into a structurally short market, which is precisely what a possibly-hiking Fed pays for, and it is the largest of my three merchant-power legs because it has the lowest multiple of the three.

The contracted, investment-grade end of the electron trade: ~31.7GW of generation, the largest carbon-free fleet in the US, nearly 1GW of new long-term nuclear contracts signed, the Microsoft Three Mile Island restart, and FY26 adjusted EPS guidance raised to $11.50-12.50. It rallied 8.0% on the week into the Microsoft and Meta multi-decade nuclear headlines yet is still -18.0% year to date and 25.6% below its high. At 24.21x forward it is the most expensive of my power legs and the $348.30 target is only 16.5% above spot, which is why it sits at 10% and not 15% - I am paying up for contract quality here, not for upside, and sizing accordingly.

Raised from 5% to 8% because it is the one leg that works whichever way the rotation resolves: Vertiv sells the power distribution and liquid cooling inside the rack, so it is paid by the same capex whether the bottleneck is priced as silicon or as electricity. It rose 9.1% this week and is +8.43% on the current leg, the best-performing survivor of the old book. I cap it at 8% rather than going larger because at roughly 33x forward it is still a high-multiple name in a tape that has spent the last month punishing exactly that, and it sits 25% below its own 52-week high.

The high-beta version of the nuclear-to-datacenter trade, bought for the cash flow rather than the accounting: $1.26B of trailing levered free cash flow against a $317.00 price and a raised 2026 guide, even though GAAP showed a Q2 loss of $92M on $959M of revenue. Mizuho initiated Outperform on Aug 24 with a $405 target after the stock had already fallen 23% year to date, and it rallied 7.1% this week off a base 29% below its high. Smallest and widest-stopped of the three power legs at 8% with a 22% stop, because merchant nuclear with a negative GAAP margin is the leg most likely to gap on a single PPA headline in either direction.

My second bits leg, deliberately in storage rather than a second DRAM name so that MU is not effectively 27% of the book in one product cycle. Seagate closed $849.28 after +6.34% on Sept 4, earned $3.18B on $12.2B of FY26 revenue with a 35.66% Q4 profit margin, and trades at 22.62x forward against a $1,125 average target (+32%). Nearline HDD is the genuinely supply-constrained tier of AI storage - the same allocation scarcity that HPE, Dell and Supermicro all flagged as limiting their AI server output - and the SK Hynix-led memory bid has been widening beyond NAND into exactly this. A 30% take-profit because at +196% year to date I am renting a cycle, not owning a compounder.

Cut from 8% to 6%, kept rather than sold. GE Vernova is the equipment side of the same electron shortage - gas turbine and grid slots are sold out for years, which is why it is +38.9% year to date and rose 3.3% this week - but at roughly 42x forward it is the most expensive thing I own, it is -5.8% over the past month, and my whole reassessment this week is that the market has stopped paying for high-multiple, back-half-loaded delivery. Consistency requires me to shrink it rather than defend it. 6% is a residual core: enough to participate if turbine pricing keeps rerating, small enough that being wrong about the multiple costs me under a point of NAV before the 18% stop.
